sessions.title: Body scan
sessions.description: Slowly notice each part of your body, from your toes to your head.
sessions.bestFor: Winding down for rest, or a quiet pause in the day

steps.say: Welcome. This is a time to rest, and there is nothing you need to do well.
Find a position that feels comfortable. You can lie down, or sit in a chair.
Keep your eyes closed, or let them rest softly on one spot. Whatever feels right for you.
You can shift or move whenever you need to, and you can pause or stop at any time.
This practice is for relaxation, so if you're unwell or distressed, please reach out to a doctor or another professional.
Now, let's begin with a few easy breaths.
Breathe in slowly, through your nose if that's comfortable.
And breathe out, a little longer.
Again, breathe in.
And breathe out, letting your shoulders drop.
One more. Breathe in.
And a slow, soft breath out.
Now let your breathing find its own rhythm. You don't need to control it.
We'll travel slowly through your body, from your toes up to your head.
You're only noticing, and softening where you can.
If any part of your body feels sore, uncomfortable or hard to feel, or you'd rather not focus on it, that's fine.
You can skip it, or rest your attention somewhere neutral, like your hands, your feet or your breath.
Bring your attention to your toes.
Notice whatever is there. Warmth, coolness, the touch of a sock or a blanket, or nothing at all.
Let your toes soften.
Now your feet. The soles, the tops, and the heels.
Allow them to rest, easy and still.
Move your attention up to your ankles.
Let them loosen.
Your calves, and your shins.
Breathe into them, and soften as you breathe out.
Your knees, soft and easy.
Your thighs, the big strong muscles at the front and the back.
Release any holding.
Now your hips, and the place where your body meets the bed or the chair.
Feel the support underneath you. You don't need to hold yourself up.
Bring your attention to your belly.
Notice it rising a little as you breathe in, and settling as you breathe out.
Let it be soft.
Your lower back.
Let it rest.
Now your chest, and your ribs.
Feel the gentle movement of your breath. Nothing to change.
Your shoulders.
Let them drop away from your ears.
Allow them to be wide and easy.
Now your arms, from the shoulders down to the elbows, and on to the wrists.
Let them be heavy and loose.
Your hands, and each finger.
Let your hands open, or rest however they like.
Now your neck, and the back of your head.
Let your head be supported.
Your jaw.
Let your teeth part a little, and let your tongue rest.
Your cheeks, and your lips.
Let them be soft.
Your eyes.
Let them rest, calm and quiet.
Your forehead, and the space between your eyebrows.
Smooth it, as if with a gentle hand.
Now let your attention rest on your whole body at once.
From your toes, all the way up to the top of your head.
Resting. Breathing. Supported.
If your mind wanders, that's completely normal. Simply come back to the feeling of your breath, with no judgement.
There's nothing to achieve here.
Let each breath be slow and easy.
You can drift off whenever you like.
If you're still awake, resting quietly like this is enough.
Rest is welcome, in whatever form it comes.

sessions.title: Sleep wind-down
sessions.description: Let the day go, slow your breath and drift into rest with gentle imagery.
sessions.bestFor: Bedtime, or any time you want to settle

steps.say: This part of your day is finished. For now, there's nothing more to do.
Settle into your bed, or a quiet seat, in whatever way feels easiest.
Close your eyes, or let them rest half open. You can pause or stop whenever you like.
Take a slow breath in.
And let it go with a soft sigh.
Once more. Breathe in.
And let it all go.
Now let the day go, a little at a time.
Whatever happened, whatever was said, it can wait until you've rested.
You did what you could, and that is enough.
Let your breath become slower.
Breathe in slowly, and out a little more slowly. Or simply follow what feels natural.
Breathe in, slowly.
And breathe out, more slowly.
Breathe in.
And breathe out.
Let your body begin to feel heavy.
If it doesn't feel heavy yet, that's fine. Just let it be as it is.
Feel your head resting on the pillow, or the back of the chair.
Feel your shoulders softening.
Your arms, warm and heavy.
Your legs, sinking into the bed or the chair.
Every part of you is supported.
Now, if you like, imagine a place that feels calm and safe.
It might be a quiet beach, a garden at dusk, a rooftop under a soft sky, or a cosy room with the rain outside.
Choose whatever feels right for you.
If pictures don't come, or this doesn't feel right, that's fine.
You can simply listen to the sounds around you, or rest your attention on your breath.
Picture it gently. Notice the light there. It is soft, and fading slowly.
Notice the air. It is mild, and just the right temperature.
Feel the ground beneath you there, soft and still warm from the day.
Listen to the sounds of that place. If you like, add the sound of gentle waves, rolling in and drifting out.
If you like, imagine each breath out as a gentle wave, or a soft breeze, moving away from you.
And each breath in as it drifts quietly back.
In, and out. Like a slow tide, or a soft breeze.
There is no hurry here.
For these few minutes, nobody needs anything from you.
Let your thoughts drift past, like clouds in a quiet sky. You don't need to follow them.
Feel the stillness settle around you.
Your breath can be slow, in its own time.
Your body may feel heavy, or it may not. Either is fine.
Your mind can grow quiet, or simply stay as it is.
Sleep can come in its own time.
If sleep hasn't come yet, resting quietly here is just as good.
Just rest here, and let the quiet hold you.
Nothing more to do. Nowhere to be.
With each breath, there is a little more space.
Rest well.

sessions.title: Unload your worries
sessions.description: Notice what is on your mind, set it down until tomorrow and choose one small next step.

steps.say: Hello. Let's take a few minutes to put things down for tonight.
Get comfortable, lying down or sitting. Close your eyes if you like.
Take a slow breath in, and a long breath out.
And again. Breathe in.
And breathe out.
Now, gently notice what is on your mind.
You don't need to fix anything. Just notice, the way you might watch traffic from a window.
Maybe there are plans, or tasks, or things you're unsure about.
If a thought comes, give it a simple name. Work. Money. Family. Tomorrow.
Let each one be there for a moment. Then let it pass.
There's no need to solve any of it right now.
Now imagine a shelf, or a table, or a basket beside you. Any safe place will do.
Take each thing on your mind, one at a time, and set it down there.
Set it down gently. It's not going anywhere.
You can pick it up again tomorrow, if you want to, with fresh eyes.
Tonight, it can rest.
Notice how your hands, your shoulders and your forehead feel now.
Let them soften a little more.
Now gently ask yourself a question. Is there one small step you could take tomorrow? Only if one is needed.
If something comes, keep it very small. A single message, a single call, or one line on a list.
Say it to yourself once, in a few simple words.
If nothing comes, that's perfectly fine.
If you like, you can write it down now, or in the morning. Or simply trust that you'll remember.
If something feels too big or too heavy, it's okay to talk to someone you trust, or to a professional.
For now, the thinking can rest.
Breathe in, and feel your body supported.
Breathe out, and let go a little more.
Let yourself settle whenever you're ready.
And if you're still awake, simply resting quietly is fine for tonight.

sessions.title: Morning intention
sessions.description: Breathe, notice how you feel, and choose one simple intention for the day.
sessions.bestFor: Starting the day with a clear, calm focus

steps.say: Good morning.
This is a relaxation practice, not a treatment, and you can pause or stop whenever you like. If you feel unwell or very distressed, please reach out to a doctor or another professional.
Find a position that feels comfortable. Sit, stand, or lie down. If you stand, keep your eyes open and stay steady. Otherwise, eyes open or closed.
Take a slow breath in, and let it go.
Once more. In, and out.
Now notice how you feel this morning. Rested, heavy, or somewhere in between.
Whatever is here is welcome.
Let your shoulders drop.
Now think about the day ahead. Not the whole list, just its shape.
Ask yourself, how would I like to meet this day?
Perhaps with patience. Perhaps with energy, kindness, or focus.
Let one word or phrase come to you. Something simple and true.
If no word comes, that is fine. Resting here is enough.
This is your intention for today. Say it quietly to yourself.
Picture, or simply think of, one moment today when it might help. A conversation, a task, or a walk.
You can return to it whenever you like. It is a guide, not a test.
Take one more slow breath in.
And out.
Feel the surface beneath you, and the sounds around you.
When you are ready, open your eyes if they were closed.
Take a breath, and step into your day.

sessions.title: Two-minute stress reset
sessions.description: Soften your body, take a few long exhales, name the feeling, and choose one small next step.
sessions.bestFor: A tense moment at work, at home, or on a break

steps.say: Pause here for a moment, if it is safe to stop where you are. You can reset.
If you are driving or cycling, please save this for later.
Stay seated, or stand and lean on a wall. Seated, eyes open or closed. Standing or out and about, keep them open.
First, let your shoulders drop, away from your ears.
Let your hands soften. Let your jaw loosen, and your tongue rest.
Breathe only as deeply as feels comfortable. If you feel light-headed, breathe normally.
Now a long breath in, through your nose if that suits you.
And a slow, long breath out, as if you are cooling a hot cup of tea.
Again. A long breath in.
And out, a little longer.
One more. Breathe in.
And a long, slow breath out.
Let your breathing return to its own pace.
Notice what you are feeling. Tense muscles, a busy mind, or a restless body.
Give it a name. Tense, rushed, worried, or whatever fits.
You might say quietly to yourself, this is stress, right now. Or use whatever name is true for you.
You are not doing anything wrong. Stress is part of being human.
Now ask yourself, what is one small thing that would help right now?
Maybe sending one message, drinking some water, or stretching, seated or standing.
Choose one, and let it be small enough to feel easy.
Take one more breath, and feel your feet or your seat beneath you.
When you are ready, open your eyes if they were closed, and take your small next step.

sessions.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
sessions.description: Use your senses to come back to the present: five things you see, four you feel, three you hear, two you smell, one you taste.
sessions.bestFor: When your mind feels busy, scattered or overwhelmed

steps.say: Begin by noticing that you are here.
Sit, stand, or lie down. Keep your eyes open or closed, whichever feels better. If you stand, keep them open and stay steady.
Please do not use this while driving or cycling. You can stop at any time and look at something neutral. Skip any step that does not feel right today.
Use your senses, counting down from five to one.
Let your next breath be a little slower.
Five things you can see. Look around slowly, and quietly name them. If your eyes are closed, or you cannot see, notice five sounds, or five places your body touches something.
Four things you can feel. The weight of your body, and your clothes on your skin.
The air on your face. Your hands, warm or cool.
Three things you can hear. Near, then far. A fan, traffic, birds, or the quiet itself. If hearing is difficult, notice three things you can feel or see instead.
Two things you can smell, if you can. Perhaps tea, soap, cooking, or fresh air. If not, imagine two smells you love, or take two slow breaths.
One thing you can taste. Notice any taste in your mouth. If you have water nearby and it suits you, take a sip. Or take one slow, full breath.
Now notice how you feel, compared with a few minutes ago.
Nothing needs to have changed. Noticing is enough.
Whenever things feel fast, you can pause and use your senses like this.
When you are ready, take a breath, and open your eyes if they were closed.

sessions.title: Gratitude pause
sessions.description: Three breaths, three simple good things from your day, and one to savour and carry forward.
sessions.bestFor: Ending a busy day, or any time you want to notice the good

steps.say: Welcome. Take a few minutes to notice what is good.
Settle into a position that feels easy. Keep your eyes open, resting on something calm, or let them close.
Begin with three breaths. Breathe in slowly, and out.
Again. In, and out.
Once more, in, and out.
Now think back over today, or the last day or two.
You are looking for small, simple good things. They do not need to be big. If three is hard to find, one is enough, and if none comes today, that is okay too.
A warm cup of chai or coffee. A kind word. A seat on the bus. Sunshine through a window.
Let the first good thing come to mind.
Now a second. It can be tiny.
And a third.
If nothing comes, rest with your breath. Simply being here, breathing, is enough.
Now choose the one that feels warmest, and stay with it for a few breaths.
Bring it to mind. Where were you? Who was there? What could you see, or hear, or feel?
Breathe in, and let the memory be clear.
Breathe out, and notice what that is like.
Notice what happens in your body. Maybe a little warmth, or a softer face.
If worry, sadness or a difficult memory shows up, that is okay. You can choose a different good thing, look around the room, or rest with your breath.
You can say a quiet thank you, in whatever way feels natural.
Take whatever you notice with you, even if it is just a little calm.
Take one last slow breath.
When you are ready, open your eyes if they were closed, and carry on with whatever comes next.

sessions.title: Kindness practice
sessions.description: A gentle, secular practice of kind wishes: for yourself, someone close, someone neutral, and everyone.
sessions.bestFor: A quiet moment of kind wishes for yourself and others

steps.say: Hello. This is a quiet time for kindness.
Sit or lie in whatever way feels comfortable. Close your eyes, lower your gaze, or keep them open, whichever feels safest.
Let one slow breath come, and go.
In this practice, I will say a few simple phrases. Repeat them silently in your mind, or use your own words.
You can skip any step if it feels hard.
If wishing others well feels like too much today, stay with the wishes for yourself. That is a good practice too.
If wishing yourself well is the hard part, you can imagine someone who cares about you offering these wishes, or simply rest with your breath.
Begin with you. Sense yourself as you are right now, or just rest on your breath.
May I be safe.
May I be well.
May I be kind to myself.
May I be at ease.
Notice whatever comes up. Warmth, nothing at all, even resistance. Let it be as it is.
Now bring to mind someone it is easy to care about. A friend, a family member, a teacher, or a pet. If that feels hard today, rest with your breath instead.
See their face, or sense their presence. Offer them the same wishes.
May you be safe.
May you be well.
May you be at ease.
Now someone neutral. Someone you see sometimes but do not know well. A neighbour, a shopkeeper, someone on your bus or train.
They want to feel safe, just like you.
May you be safe.
May you be well.
May you be at ease.
Now widen your attention, to everyone. Your street, your town, people far away, in every village and city.
May we all be safe.
May we all be well.
May we all be at ease.
Rest in the stillness for a moment.
Place a hand on your chest or belly, if you like.
May I be gentle with myself today.
Take a slow breath in, and out. Notice the surface beneath you, and the sounds in the room.
When you are ready, let your eyes open if they were closed.

sessions.title: Focus reset
sessions.description: A short pause to clear mental clutter and choose your one next task.
sessions.bestFor: Between tasks, or when your attention feels scattered

steps.say: Let's reset. Just three minutes.
Sit or stand, whichever suits you, with your back tall but easy and your feet resting wherever is comfortable.
Rest your hands, and let your shoulders drop. Close your eyes, or lower your gaze to a spot in front of you.
We'll take three steady breaths.
Breathe in slowly, through your nose if you can.
And breathe out, slowly and easily.
Breathe in, comfortably.
And breathe out, letting your body settle.
One more. Breathe in.
And breathe out.
Now, notice how many tabs are open in your mind.
Emails, messages, errands, half finished jobs.
One by one, picture each tab closing.
They're not lost. You can open them again later.
For now, let them go quiet.
Now ask yourself: what is the one small thing that is most worth doing next?
Choose just one, and keep it clear.
Say it silently, in a few simple words.
Picture yourself starting it. The very first move.
Now bring your attention back to the room.
Wiggle your fingers and toes, or move in any small way that suits you.
Take one deeper breath in, if that feels good.
Breathe out, and open your eyes when you're ready.
Whenever you're ready, begin with that one small step.

sessions.title: Mindful eating
sessions.description: Slow down and enjoy a meal or snack, with curiosity and no judgement.
sessions.bestFor: The start of a meal or snack

steps.say: Before you start eating, pause for a moment.
This works with a full meal or a small snack. Any food at all, including soft or simple foods.
Sit down if you can, or stay as you are. Set your phone down within reach, screen up if you're following the captions.
Take a slow breath in, and a slow breath out.
Whatever you eat, and however you eat it, is welcome here. There are no good or bad foods in this practice.
If you have a complicated relationship with food, go gently, and skip anything that doesn't feel right.
Begin by looking.
Notice the colours, the shapes, and the steam if there is any.
Now notice the smell.
Bring the food a little closer, and breathe in.
If you can't see or smell your food, notice its warmth, and how the plate or spoon feels in your hand.
Check in with your body, if that feels helpful. Are you hungry, or not so much? Either answer is fine.
Now take your first bite. Make it a small one.
Before you chew, notice the food resting in your mouth.
Chew slowly. What flavours do you notice? Sweet, salty, sour, spicy, or something else?
What about the texture? Soft, crunchy, creamy, or smooth?
Swallow when you're ready.
Let each bite be slow and unhurried, at whatever pace suits you.
Take your time. I'll be quiet while you eat, and invite you to pause in a little while.
Now pause, wherever you are in your meal.
Rest your fork or spoon, or lower the food in your hands. Take a breath.
How does your body feel now? Are you still hungry, or comfortably satisfied?
Whatever you notice is simply information. There is nothing to judge.
Carry on, if you wish, or stop if you're done. Both are fine.
If you've been advised to eat a certain amount, or at set times, keep to that. Hunger and fullness are only one kind of information.
Take a moment to thank the food, and the people who grew it, cooked it or shared it with you.
And be kind to your body. It's doing its best for you.
Take a breath, and bring your attention back to the room.
When you're ready, carry on with your meal, or with your day.

breathing.name: Box breathing
breathing.description: Breathe in, hold, breathe out, hold, each for four counts. Good for steadying your focus.

breathing.name: 4-7-8 breathing
breathing.description: A slow pattern with a long exhale for winding down. Beginners can start with three rounds.

breathing.name: Coherent breathing
breathing.description: A calm, even rhythm of about six breaths a minute.

breathing.name: Long exhale
breathing.description: Breathe out a little longer than you breathe in. A gentle first pattern for easing tension.

sounds.name: White noise
sounds.description: An even hiss that covers background sounds.

sounds.name: Pink noise
sounds.description: Softer than white noise, with more low tones.

sounds.name: Brown noise
sounds.description: A deep, rumbling noise that many people find calming.

sounds.name: Ocean waves
sounds.description: Slow, generated waves rolling in and out.

sounds.name: Focus tone
sounds.description: A soft, slowly shifting drone for concentration.
